1.title: Aerodynamics and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)
1.scope: Lift, drag, pressure distribution, turbulent flows, flow separation, stall, shock waves, wakes, RANS, LES and DNS
1.classical: The required governing equations include the Navier–Stokes equations, continuity equation, conservation of momentum equation, total energy equation, compressible Euler equations, ideal gas equation of state, real-gas equations of state where appropriate, Reynolds transport theorem, Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations, Favre-averaged conservation equations, vorticity transport equation, boundary-layer equations, Prandtl boundary-layer equations, Bernoulli equation within its validity limits, potential-flow equation, Laplace equation, compressible potential-flow equation, circulation theorem, Kutta–Joukowski lift theorem, Prandtl lifting-line theory, lifting-surface integral equations, thin-airfoil theory, Prandtl–Glauert compressibility correction, Rankine–Hugoniot jump conditions, normal and oblique shock relations, entropy transport equation, turbulent kinetic energy transport equation, Reynolds stress transport equations, and transition intermittency transport equations.
1.hybrid: Applicable hybrid formulations include hybrid RANS–LES equations, Detached Eddy Simulation formulations, Delayed Detached Eddy Simulation formulations, Improved Delayed Detached Eddy Simulation formulations, wall-modelled LES formulations, coupled Eulerian–Lagrangian particle transport, immersed-boundary formulations, actuator-line and actuator-disk momentum source formulations, moving-grid Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian conservation equations, overset-grid conservative interpolation, coupled CFD–structural displacement equations, and physics-informed data-assisted turbulence closure formulations.
1.models: The models include Spalart–Allmaras, standard and realizable k–epsilon, standard and SST k–omega, Reynolds Stress Models, transition SST, gamma–Re-theta transition, LES subgrid-scale models, dynamic Smagorinsky, WALE, DES, DDES, IDDES, DNS, vortex lattice models, panel methods, lifting-line models, free-vortex wake models, compressible finite-volume solvers, high-resolution shock-capturing schemes, and wall-resolved or wall-modelled turbulence simulations. Aircraft-specific applications require high-lift aerodynamic models, wing–fuselage interference models, rotor wake models, stall and post-stall models, shock–boundary-layer interaction models, and aerodynamic icing degradation models.
1.ic: Specify the initial velocity field, pressure field, temperature field, density distribution, Mach number, Reynolds number, angle of attack, sideslip angle, aircraft translational and rotational velocities, turbulence kinetic energy, turbulence dissipation rate or specific dissipation rate, eddy viscosity, turbulence intensity, turbulence length scale, boundary-layer state, initial vortex structures, initial shock-wave locations where relevant, and initial flow-field perturbations. For helicopter simulations, additionally initialise rotor angular velocity, rotor azimuth, blade pitch distribution, induced velocity field, rotor wake geometry, blade flapping state and rotor–fuselage interaction field.
1.bc: Prescribe freestream velocity, pressure, temperature, density, flow direction, atmospheric turbulence and far-field conditions. Apply impermeability and appropriate no-slip or slip conditions at aircraft surfaces, specified wall thermal conditions, moving-wall or rotating-frame conditions for rotor blades and propellers, periodic or phase-lagged conditions where appropriate, inlet total pressure and temperature for engine intakes, outlet static pressure or non-reflecting conditions, symmetry conditions where physically justified, and ground-wall conditions for takeoff, landing and hover simulations. Specify moving-mesh or overset-grid interface conditions and suitable acoustic or characteristic far-field conditions for compressible flow.
1.calibration: Calibrate turbulence closure coefficients, transition onset parameters, wall roughness effects, near-wall treatments, separation behaviour, aerodynamic interference corrections and compressibility-sensitive modelling parameters against independently measured aerodynamic datasets. Use pressure distributions, lift and drag measurements, pitching moments, boundary-layer profiles, skin-friction measurements, wake velocity surveys, particle image velocimetry, laser Doppler velocimetry and established wind-tunnel measurements. Include low- and high-Reynolds-number conditions, attached and separated flows, stall onset, post-stall behaviour, shock-wave interactions and representative rotorcraft flow regimes. Distinguish empirical coefficient calibration from numerical solver configuration, and avoid adjusting universal turbulence-model coefficients merely to match individual aircraft cases.
1.verification: Perform code verification using analytical solutions, manufactured solutions and established numerical benchmarks; assess spatial and temporal discretisation convergence, grid refinement, iterative convergence, residual reduction, global and local conservation of mass, momentum and energy, boundary-condition consistency, numerical stability and sensitivity to mesh topology. Verify turbulence-model implementation, wall-distance calculations, moving meshes, rotating reference frames, overset-grid interpolation, compressible-flow shock capturing, parallel reproducibility and force integration. Quantify discretisation and iterative uncertainties through systematic refinement studies and suitable convergence estimators.
1.validation: Validate predicted lift, drag, moments, surface pressures, stall characteristics, shock locations, wake structures, vortex trajectories and unsteady aerodynamic loads against independent wind-tunnel and flight-test datasets. Suitable benchmark families include the NASA Common Research Model, NASA Common Research Model High-Lift configuration, NASA High-Lift Prediction Workshop datasets, AGARD aerodynamic cases, canonical turbulent boundary-layer experiments and independently measured rotor flow fields. Evaluate accuracy across the operating envelope, including off-design conditions, and document systematic biases, uncertainty intervals, validation-domain limitations and extrapolation risks.
1.inputs: Aircraft three-dimensional geometry; wing, fuselage, empennage, rotor and control-surface geometries; computational mesh; mesh refinement regions; airfoil profiles; surface roughness; flight altitude; freestream velocity; Mach number; Reynolds number; air density; pressure; temperature; viscosity; angle of attack; sideslip angle; turbulence intensity; turbulence length scale; boundary conditions; initial conditions; wall treatment; turbulence models; transition models; compressibility models; numerical discretisation schemes; solver convergence tolerances; time-step size; moving-body conditions; rotor rotational speed; control-surface deflections; and atmospheric conditions.
1.outputs: Three-dimensional velocity fields; pressure fields; temperature fields; density fields; turbulence quantities; wall shear stress; surface pressure coefficient; skin-friction coefficient; lift, drag and side-force coefficients; pitching, rolling and yawing moment coefficients; lift-to-drag ratio; aerodynamic centre; centre of pressure; boundary-layer thickness; separation and reattachment locations; shock-wave positions; vortex structures; wake velocity deficits; vorticity; wall heat flux; aerodynamic load distributions; stall characteristics; aerodynamic polars; time histories; residual histories; force and moment convergence; flow visualisations; and integrated aerodynamic performance reports.
1.geometry: The application shall accept complete aircraft external geometry, including fuselages, wings, winglets, stabilisers, flaps, slats, spoilers, nacelles, engine inlets, exhaust nozzles, propellers, rotor blades, rotor hubs, tail rotors and other aerodynamic surfaces. Conventional CAD imports shall include STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS and JT, while unconventional imports shall include STL, OBJ, PLY, 3MF, glTF, reconstructed point-cloud surfaces, parametric airfoils, procedural wing surfaces, implicit geometries and voxel-derived geometries. Computational meshes shall be accepted through CGNS, Gmsh, SU2, Fluent, OpenFOAM, VTK, Plot3D, Tecplot and other compatible structured or unstructured mesh formats. The geometry-processing system shall support watertight surface reconstruction, aerodynamic domain generation, boundary-layer meshing, moving meshes, overset grids and adaptive mesh refinement for realistic subsonic, transonic, supersonic, rotorcraft and unconventional aircraft configurations.

2.title: Structural Mechanics and Finite Element Analysis (FEA)
2.scope: Stress, strain, deformation, structural loads, buckling, nonlinear mechanics and structural integrity
2.classical: The governing equations include the Cauchy momentum equation, static equilibrium equations, strain–displacement compatibility equations, Hooke’s law, generalized Hooke’s law, linear elasticity equations, nonlinear elasticity equations, Green–Lagrange strain relations, Euler–Bernoulli beam equations, Timoshenko beam equations, Kirchhoff–Love plate equations, Mindlin–Reissner plate equations, classical shell equations, von Kármán large-deflection plate equations, Saint-Venant torsion equations, Euler buckling equation, geometric stiffness equations, principle of virtual work, minimum potential energy principle, Hamilton’s principle, and finite element weak-form equilibrium equations.
2.hybrid: These include coupled structural–thermal equations, nonlinear contact equilibrium equations, geometric and material nonlinear finite element formulations, multibody–finite element coupling, structural–aerodynamic load-transfer equations, explicit–implicit time integration, mixed displacement–pressure formulations, reduced-order structural equations, and multiscale homogenisation formulations.
2.models: The models include linear and nonlinear finite element models, beam models, shell models, solid-element models, composite structural models, geometrically exact beam models, corotational finite element models, elastic–plastic constitutive models, hyperelastic models where applicable, contact mechanics models, buckling models, post-buckling models, damage mechanics models, and aircraft structural load-path models. Specialised models cover wing spars, ribs, skins, fuselage frames, rotor blades, rotor hubs, engine mounts, landing gear and structural joints.
2.ic: Define the initial displacement, velocity, acceleration, stress, strain, temperature, material state, residual stress, geometric imperfections, structural preload, gravitational loading, centrifugal loading, aircraft mass distribution and initial contact configuration. For composite structures, initialise laminate orientation, ply properties, manufacturing residual stresses and pre-existing damage where applicable.
2.bc: Specify displacement constraints, rotational constraints, structural supports, applied forces, moments, pressure loads, aerodynamic pressure distributions, inertial loads, gravitational forces, centrifugal forces, thermal loads, contact constraints, joint stiffness, attachment conditions and interface compatibility. Represent wing–fuselage connections, rotor hub attachments, engine mounts, landing gear supports, fasteners and other structural interfaces using physically appropriate stiffness and load-transfer conditions rather than automatically assuming perfectly fixed connections.
2.calibration: Calibrate elastic moduli, Poisson ratios, shear moduli, plasticity parameters, hardening behaviour, damping coefficients, joint stiffness, contact friction, fastener stiffness, material anisotropy and structural boundary-condition representations using coupon tests, subcomponent tests, static loading experiments and modal measurements. Determine temperature-dependent material properties, composite laminate stiffness and structural connection behaviour using independently measured data.
2.verification: Verify element formulations, interpolation functions, numerical integration, stiffness and mass matrices, stress recovery, constraint enforcement, contact algorithms and nonlinear solution procedures. Conduct patch tests, rigid-body mode checks, mesh-convergence studies, equilibrium checks, strain-energy consistency assessments, element distortion sensitivity analyses and comparisons with analytical beam, plate, shell and elasticity solutions. Verify large-deformation calculations, buckling eigenvalues, nonlinear material response and transient structural dynamics.
2.validation: Validate displacement fields, strains, stresses, load distributions, buckling loads, failure locations and structural stiffness against laboratory tests, full-scale structural tests, ground tests and aircraft component qualification experiments. Compare predictions with measured wing bending, fuselage deformation, landing gear loads, rotor blade deflections and composite structural responses. Demonstrate predictive accuracy at component, subassembly and full-aircraft levels without recalibrating against the validation results.
2.inputs: Structural CAD geometry; structural mesh; material elastic properties; density; Poisson's ratio; yield strength; ultimate strength; plasticity curves; structural thicknesses; beam and shell properties; stiffener geometry; joint and fastener properties; composite layups; contact definitions; constraints; supports; aerodynamic loads; inertial loads; gravitational loads; engine thrust loads; rotor loads; cabin pressure; thermal loads; load combinations; damping properties; nonlinear material models; and solution controls.
2.outputs: Displacement fields; strain tensors; stress tensors; von Mises stresses; principal stresses; shear stresses; reaction forces; internal forces; bending moments; torsional moments; structural deflections; stiffness matrices; stress concentration factors; yield margins; ultimate strength margins; load paths; buckling eigenvalues; buckling mode shapes; nonlinear load–displacement curves; contact pressures; joint loads; structural reserve factors; critical failure locations; and structural integrity reports.
2.geometry: The application shall import structural geometry representing wings, fuselage frames, ribs, spars, stringers, bulkheads, landing gear, rotor blades, rotor hubs, engine mounts, joints and complete aircraft assemblies. Conventional formats shall include STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, JT and compatible native CAD assembly representations, while unconventional representations shall include STL, OBJ, PLY, voxel-derived solids, lattice structures, implicit solids and topology-optimised geometries. Structural mesh imports shall include Nastran BDF/NAS, Abaqus INP, ANSYS CDB, Exodus II, MED, UNV, Gmsh and VTK-compatible finite element datasets. The system shall preserve structural connectivity, element types, thickness definitions, material orientations, contact interfaces, assembly relationships and local coordinate systems wherever those attributes are available.

3.title: Aeroelasticity and Fluid–Structure Interaction (FSI)
3.scope: Flutter, divergence, control reversal, aerodynamic–structural coupling and aeroelastic instability
3.classical: The governing equations include the coupled aerodynamic–structural equations of motion, linearised structural dynamic equations, Euler–Lagrange equations, unsteady aerodynamic integral equations, Theodorsen unsteady airfoil theory, Wagner indicial lift formulation, Küssner gust-response formulation, doublet-lattice aerodynamic equations, piston theory for suitable supersonic applications, flutter eigenvalue equations, divergence equilibrium equations, control reversal relations, and modal superposition equations.
3.hybrid: These include partitioned CFD–CSD coupling equations, monolithic fluid–structure equations, Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian fluid equations, interface displacement compatibility equations, interface traction equilibrium equations, strongly coupled and loosely coupled time-marching formulations, nonlinear aeroservoelastic equations, reduced-order aerodynamic–structural coupling, and fluid–structure–thermal interaction formulations.
3.models: The models include linear flutter models, p–k flutter models, k-method flutter models, nonlinear time-domain flutter models, doublet-lattice models, CFD-based aeroelastic models, finite element structural dynamics models, rotor aeroelastic models, geometrically exact rotor blade models, transonic aeroelastic models, limit-cycle oscillation models, gust-response models, and coupled control-system aeroelastic models.
3.ic: Specify the initial aerodynamic flow field, structural displacement, structural velocity, structural acceleration, elastic mode amplitudes, modal velocities, initial stress state, structural damping, aircraft flight speed, Mach number, dynamic pressure, angle of attack, rotor rotational speed, blade deformation, control surface position and initial aerodynamic perturbations.
3.bc: Apply aerodynamic freestream and far-field conditions, structural support and attachment constraints, fluid–structure displacement compatibility, velocity continuity, traction equilibrium, aerodynamic pressure transfer, structural deformation feedback, control surface hinge constraints, rotor hub boundary conditions, prescribed or free rigid-body motion, and non-reflecting aerodynamic boundaries where necessary. Ensure conservation and consistent transfer of interface loads and motion between the aerodynamic and structural domains.
3.calibration: Calibrate structural stiffness distributions, modal damping, aerodynamic influence coefficients, unsteady aerodynamic parameters, joint flexibility, control-surface hinge characteristics and fluid–structure coupling parameters using ground vibration tests, wind-tunnel aeroelastic measurements and instrumented structural tests. Establish mass distributions, mode shapes, natural frequencies and aerodynamic loading characteristics independently.
3.verification: Verify coupling consistency between aerodynamic and structural meshes, displacement transfer, force transfer, energy conservation, interface equilibrium, temporal synchronisation, coupling convergence and numerical stability. Conduct mesh and time-step convergence studies, verify modal representations and compare predicted flutter boundaries and divergence behaviour with analytical aeroelastic benchmarks. Examine the effects of partitioned versus strongly coupled solution procedures and artificial numerical damping.
3.validation: Validate flutter speeds, flutter frequencies, aeroelastic damping, divergence boundaries, control reversal, limit-cycle oscillations, wing deformation and gust-induced responses against aeroelastic wind-tunnel tests, ground vibration measurements and carefully controlled flight flutter tests. Include rotor blade aeroelasticity, whirl flutter and coupled rotor–fuselage behaviour where applicable. Confirm that the computational framework correctly predicts stability margins and their sensitivity to operating conditions.
3.inputs: Aerodynamic geometry; structural finite element model; mass distribution; stiffness distribution; structural damping; aerodynamic coefficients; unsteady aerodynamic models; flight speed; altitude; Mach number; air density; dynamic pressure; modal frequencies; mode shapes; control-surface properties; rotor blade flexibility; aerodynamic–structural interface definitions; mesh-motion settings; coupling algorithms; time steps; and convergence tolerances.
3.outputs: Flutter onset speed; flutter frequency; flutter damping; divergence speed; control reversal speed; aeroelastic deformation; coupled pressure and displacement fields; modal participation factors; aeroelastic eigenvalues; stability boundaries; aerodynamic load redistribution; limit-cycle oscillation amplitudes; blade deflection histories; structural vibration responses; coupled transient responses; flutter margin diagrams; and aeroelastic stability envelopes.
3.geometry: The application shall accept coupled aerodynamic and structural geometry, including flexible wings, rotor blades, control surfaces, propellers, fuselage structures and deformable aerodynamic components. STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS and JT shall provide conventional CAD geometry, while STL, OBJ, PLY, procedural surfaces, morphing geometries, implicit geometries and reconstructed surfaces shall provide unconventional representations. Aerodynamic meshes shall be imported through CGNS, SU2, Fluent, OpenFOAM, Gmsh and VTK, while structural meshes shall be imported through Nastran, Abaqus, ANSYS, Exodus II and MED formats. The software shall support nonmatching fluid and structural meshes, moving boundaries, deformation transfer, conservative load transfer and coupling-interface identification, subject to numerical compatibility and conservation checks.

4.title: Flight Dynamics, Stability and Control
4.scope: Six-degree-of-freedom flight simulation, longitudinal and lateral stability, manoeuvrability, trim and handling qualities
4.classical: The equations include Newton–Euler rigid-body equations, six-degree-of-freedom aircraft equations of motion, translational and rotational momentum equations, Euler rotational kinematic equations, quaternion attitude propagation equations, direction cosine matrix relations, aerodynamic force and moment equations, longitudinal and lateral-directional linearised state equations, aircraft trim equations, stability derivative equations, characteristic eigenvalue equations, short-period approximation equations, phugoid approximation equations, Dutch-roll equations, roll subsidence equations, spiral stability equations, and flight-path kinematic equations.
4.hybrid: These include nonlinear six-degree-of-freedom models coupled to CFD aerodynamic databases, flight dynamics–aeroelastic coupling, flight dynamics–propulsion coupling, nonlinear state estimation equations, gain-scheduled state-space formulations, stochastic gust-response equations, differential–algebraic aircraft system equations, and hybrid discrete–continuous flight mode formulations.
4.models: The models include nonlinear six-degree-of-freedom flight simulation models, linear state-space models, longitudinal and lateral stability models, aircraft trim models, aerodynamic coefficient lookup models, nonlinear stall and post-stall models, atmospheric turbulence models, Dryden turbulence models, von Kármán turbulence models, handling qualities models, pilot-in-the-loop models, helicopter rotorcraft flight dynamics models, and flight envelope protection models.
4.ic: Specify aircraft geographic position, altitude, translational velocity, angular velocity, Euler angles or quaternion attitude, mass, centre of gravity, inertia tensor, fuel state, engine operating state, control surface deflections, rotor collective and cyclic pitch settings, rotor speed, atmospheric conditions, initial flight-path angle, initial heading, and initial trim or disturbed flight condition.
4.bc: Classical spatial boundary conditions are generally not required for ordinary six-degree-of-freedom flight dynamics. Instead, prescribe atmospheric and gravitational environments, terrain elevation, runway or landing surface geometry, aircraft operating-envelope limits, maximum and minimum control deflections, actuator rate limits, engine thrust limits, rotor operating limits, aerodynamic validity limits, flight-path constraints and terminal flight-state requirements. Include ground-contact conditions when modelling takeoff, landing or ground operations.
4.calibration: Calibrate aerodynamic stability derivatives, control derivatives, aircraft mass properties, moments of inertia, actuator characteristics, control effectiveness, damping parameters and propulsion response using wind-tunnel measurements, flight-test system identification and ground-based measurements. Determine trim characteristics and control response parameters over representative airspeeds, altitudes, configurations and loading conditions.
4.verification: Verify six-degree-of-freedom rigid-body dynamics, coordinate transformations, reference-frame conventions, rotational kinematics, force and moment integration, inertia coupling, numerical time integration and trim solution convergence. Check conservation properties where applicable, equilibrium conditions, small-disturbance linearisation, eigenvalue calculations and agreement between nonlinear and linearised models near trim. Verify stability derivatives and control system interfaces.
4.validation: Validate predicted longitudinal and lateral-directional responses, short-period motion, phugoid behaviour, Dutch roll, roll response, spiral stability, manoeuvrability, trim settings and handling qualities against instrumented flight tests. Compare simulated responses with measured pilot control inputs, aircraft accelerations, angular rates, attitudes, trajectories and control-surface deflections. Include helicopter hover, transition flight and rotorcraft handling qualities where applicable.
4.inputs: Aircraft mass; centre of gravity; inertia tensor; aerodynamic force and moment coefficients; aerodynamic stability derivatives; control derivatives; propulsion characteristics; thrust-vector orientation; control-surface geometry; rotor control characteristics; flight speed; altitude; initial position; attitude; angular velocity; translational velocity; atmospheric conditions; wind disturbances; pilot control commands; and aircraft configuration.
4.outputs: Six-degree-of-freedom trajectories; aircraft position; velocity; acceleration; Euler angles or quaternions; angular rates; aerodynamic forces; aerodynamic moments; trimmed flight conditions; trim control settings; longitudinal and lateral-directional stability derivatives; eigenvalues; damping ratios; natural frequencies; phugoid characteristics; short-period characteristics; Dutch-roll characteristics; spiral stability; roll response; manoeuvre response; control effectiveness; stability margins; handling qualities metrics; and flight-state time histories.
4.geometry: The application shall accept complete aircraft geometry and simplified aerodynamic representations of wings, fuselage, tail surfaces, control surfaces, rotor systems, propulsion units and landing gear. Conventional CAD formats shall include STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS and JT, while unconventional geometry shall include STL, OBJ, PLY, glTF, procedural aircraft configurations, reduced-order geometric models and parametric lifting surfaces. Aerodynamic reference meshes may be imported through CGNS, SU2, Gmsh and VTK, while flight-dynamics-specific inputs shall additionally include aircraft mass properties, aerodynamic coefficient databases, control effectiveness data and inertia tensors. The system shall derive or associate the necessary reference geometry and geometric properties for six-degree-of-freedom aircraft simulation.

5.title: Aircraft Performance and Flight Envelope
5.scope: Takeoff, landing, climb, cruise, descent, maximum speed, range, endurance, service ceiling and flight limitations
5.classical: The required equations include aircraft force equilibrium equations, thrust–drag balance equations, lift–weight balance equations, equations of motion along the flight path, specific excess power equations, aircraft energy equations, Breguet range equation, Breguet endurance relations, rate-of-climb equations, service ceiling relations, takeoff ground-roll equations, landing ground-roll equations, turning flight equations, load-factor equations, stall speed equations, manoeuvre envelope relations, gust load relations, and payload–range equations.
5.hybrid: These include coupled flight performance–engine cycle equations, atmospheric–aerodynamic performance equations, energy-based trajectory optimisation formulations, hybrid-electric energy balance equations, stochastic mission performance equations, and aircraft performance models coupled to flight control and thermal constraints.
5.models: The models include takeoff performance models, landing performance models, climb and descent models, cruise performance models, fuel burn models, thrust lapse models, drag polar models, flight envelope models, payload–range models, hot-and-high performance models, one-engine-inoperative performance models, helicopter hover ceiling models, helicopter height–velocity envelope models, and mission energy management models.
5.ic: Specify aircraft takeoff mass, payload, fuel quantity, centre of gravity, altitude, airspeed, atmospheric pressure, ambient temperature, wind speed, runway condition, engine thrust or power setting, aircraft configuration, flap position, landing gear position, rotor speed and initial flight phase. For helicopters, additionally define hover height, rotor collective pitch, rotor disk loading and initial induced-flow state.
5.bc: Prescribe atmospheric variation with altitude, wind and turbulence environments, runway length, runway slope, runway friction, obstacle clearance requirements, aircraft structural load limits, maximum operating speeds, stall boundaries, engine power limits, rotor thrust limits, rotor speed limits, maximum allowable temperatures, fuel reserve constraints and permissible flight-envelope boundaries. For performance maps rather than transient trajectories, these are operating constraints and envelope definitions.
5.calibration: Calibrate aircraft drag polars, propulsion performance maps, fuel consumption characteristics, high-lift performance, ground rolling resistance, braking coefficients, atmospheric corrections and aircraft weight models using wind-tunnel data, engine tests, ground tests and flight performance measurements. Determine configuration-specific performance corrections for landing gear, flaps, external stores and aircraft loading.
5.verification: Verify force balance, power balance, energy accounting, fuel mass integration, atmospheric property calculations, climb and descent computations, runway performance calculations and flight-envelope boundary detection. Compare numerical performance calculations with analytical limiting cases, independently implemented performance methods and established aircraft performance calculations. Verify interpolation of aerodynamic and engine performance tables.
5.validation: Validate takeoff distance, landing distance, climb rate, cruise speed, range, endurance, service ceiling, maximum operating limits and payload–range characteristics against measured flight-test data and approved performance information. For helicopters, validate hover ceiling, hover power, vertical climb performance, autorotation characteristics and height–velocity envelope predictions. Quantify performance errors across aircraft mass, altitude, temperature and atmospheric conditions.
5.inputs: Aircraft aerodynamic polars; mass and loading; engine thrust or shaft power maps; propeller or rotor efficiency maps; fuel capacity; fuel consumption characteristics; altitude; atmospheric temperature; runway length; runway slope; runway condition; wind; aircraft configuration; flap settings; landing gear configuration; climb schedule; cruise schedule; structural load limits; operating speed limits; and engine failure conditions.
5.outputs: Takeoff distance; landing distance; balanced field length where applicable; takeoff speeds; stall speeds; climb rate; climb gradient; cruise speed; maximum level-flight speed; service ceiling; absolute ceiling; range; endurance; fuel consumption; specific range; payload–range curves; excess thrust; excess power; turn radius; turn rate; load-factor limits; V–n diagrams; altitude–Mach envelopes; operating speed envelopes; and performance limitation charts.
5.geometry: The application shall accept complete aircraft configurations, including wings, fuselages, empennages, propulsion installations, control surfaces and landing gear, using STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS and JT. Unconventional geometry shall include STL, OBJ, PLY, parametric aircraft layouts, procedural wing and fuselage definitions, conceptual design geometry and reduced-order aerodynamic models. Compatible aerodynamic meshes shall be accepted through CGNS, SU2, Fluent, OpenFOAM, Gmsh and VTK when higher-fidelity performance predictions are required. The application shall combine geometric information with mass properties, propulsion characteristics, aerodynamic databases and environmental conditions to calculate takeoff, landing, climb, cruise, descent, range, endurance and flight-envelope characteristics.

6.title: Rotorcraft Aerodynamics and Aeromechanics
6.scope: Rotor thrust, torque, induced flow, blade flapping, lead–lag dynamics, dynamic stall and blade–vortex interactions
6.classical: The governing equations include rotor momentum theory, blade element theory, blade element momentum theory, actuator-disk momentum equations, rotor thrust and torque equations, induced velocity equations, rotor inflow equations, blade flapping equations, blade lead–lag equations, blade feathering equations, rotating beam equations, centrifugal stiffening equations, Coriolis acceleration relations, Euler–Lagrange rotor dynamics equations, vortex filament equations, Biot–Savart law, Kelvin circulation theorem, and dynamic stall state equations.
6.hybrid: These include coupled blade element–dynamic inflow formulations, rotor CFD–structural dynamics equations, free-wake–blade structural coupling, rotor–fuselage aerodynamic interaction equations, rotor–tail rotor interaction formulations, coupled multibody–elastic rotor equations, and nonlinear rotorcraft flight dynamics coupling.
6.models: The models include blade element momentum models, Pitt–Peters dynamic inflow models, Peters–He finite-state inflow models, prescribed-wake models, free-vortex wake models, lifting-line rotor models, Leishman–Beddoes dynamic stall models, ONERA dynamic stall models, comprehensive rotorcraft aeromechanics models, elastic rotor blade models, rotor–fuselage interference models, coaxial rotor models, tandem rotor models, and autorotation models.
6.ic: Specify rotor angular velocity, blade azimuth, collective pitch, longitudinal cyclic pitch, lateral cyclic pitch, blade flapping angles, lead–lag angles, blade torsional deformation, blade velocities, rotor induced-flow distribution, initial wake geometry, blade aerodynamic states, helicopter forward speed, climb or descent rate, fuselage attitude and tail rotor operating state.
6.bc: Prescribe rotor hub translational and rotational constraints, blade root articulation or elastic restraint, pitch-link actuation, blade surface no-slip conditions for viscous CFD, atmospheric freestream conditions, ground-effect boundaries, rotor wake far-field conditions, rotor–fuselage interaction conditions, tail rotor inflow conditions, blade structural attachment conditions and aerodynamic–structural interface compatibility. Include periodicity conditions only when the rotor configuration and operating state justify them.
6.calibration: Calibrate rotor blade aerodynamic polars, dynamic stall parameters, induced inflow characteristics, blade structural stiffness, blade damping, hinge properties, rotor wake representations and rotor–fuselage interference parameters using rotor test rigs, hover stands, wind-tunnel tests and instrumented helicopter flight measurements. Include advancing-blade compressibility, retreating-blade stall, blade flapping, lead–lag motion and blade–vortex interaction.
6.verification: Verify rotating-frame dynamics, blade element integration, rotor momentum conservation, centrifugal and Coriolis force calculations, blade structural equations, rotor wake convection, induced velocity calculations and aerodynamic–structural coupling. Check convergence with respect to azimuthal resolution, radial blade discretisation, wake discretisation, time step and rotor revolutions. Verify blade flapping, lead–lag and torsional modes against independently calculated solutions.
6.validation: Validate rotor thrust, torque, power, blade deflection, flapping response, lead–lag response, wake geometry, induced velocity, dynamic stall and blade–vortex interactions against rotorcraft experimental datasets. Suitable reference programmes include NASA and Army rotorcraft experiments, the HART rotor test campaigns, UH-60 rotor measurements and independent hover and forward-flight rotor performance tests. Assess hover, climb, descent, forward flight and transitional flight separately.
6.inputs: Main rotor diameter; blade count; blade chord; twist; taper; sweep; airfoil distributions; rotor solidity; rotational speed; hub geometry; blade mass; blade inertia; blade stiffness; blade damping; collective pitch; cyclic pitch; shaft tilt; flight velocity; air density; inflow conditions; rotor wake models; tail rotor geometry; rotor–fuselage separation; and blade dynamic stall characteristics.
6.outputs: Rotor thrust; torque; power; induced velocity; induced power; rotor thrust coefficient; rotor torque coefficient; rotor power coefficient; blade sectional aerodynamic loads; blade flapping angles; lead–lag motion; blade torsion; rotor inflow distributions; dynamic stall regions; advancing-blade compressibility effects; retreating-blade stall boundaries; rotor wake trajectories; blade–vortex interaction locations; hub forces; hub moments; rotor trim conditions; rotor vibration harmonics; and rotor stability characteristics.
6.geometry: The application shall import helicopter main rotor blades, tail rotor blades, rotor hubs, swashplates, rotor masts, fuselages, stabilisers and complete rotorcraft configurations. Conventional CAD geometry shall include STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS and JT, while unconventional geometry shall include STL, OBJ, PLY, parametric rotor blade definitions, blade twist and chord distributions, reconstructed blade surfaces, procedural rotor geometries and implicit blade representations. Computational mesh imports shall include CGNS, Gmsh, Fluent, OpenFOAM, SU2, VTK and compatible moving-mesh representations. The application shall support rotating reference frames, sliding interfaces, overset meshes, deforming blade meshes, free-wake representations and coupled rotor structural meshes for hover, forward flight, autorotation, blade–vortex interaction and dynamic stall analysis.

7.title: Propulsion and Engine Performance
7.scope: Turbofan, turbojet, turboprop, turboshaft, piston engines, compressors, turbines and combustion
7.classical: The equations include conservation of mass, momentum and energy equations, first and second laws of thermodynamics, Brayton cycle equations, Otto cycle equations, Diesel cycle equations where applicable, ideal and real gas equations of state, compressor energy equations, turbine energy equations, nozzle flow equations, thrust equations, combustion energy equations, chemical species conservation equations, reaction-rate equations, heat-transfer equations, compressor and turbine efficiency relations, shaft power balance equations, and engine spool dynamics equations.
7.hybrid: These include coupled zero-dimensional engine cycle and three-dimensional CFD formulations, compressor–combustor–turbine coupling, engine–airframe aerodynamic interaction equations, gas turbine–electric motor power balance equations, battery–generator hybrid propulsion equations, hydrogen combustion–thermal coupling, and engine health state estimation equations.
7.models: The models include turbojet, turbofan, turboprop, turboshaft and piston engine cycle models, compressor maps, turbine maps, combustor models, chemical kinetics models, engine transient models, engine inlet distortion models, turbine cooling models, engine structural models, engine emissions models, and hybrid-electric propulsion models.
7.ic: Specify engine shaft rotational speeds, compressor operating state, turbine operating state, combustion chamber pressure and temperature, fuel flow rate, air mass flow rate, fuel–air ratio, combustor species concentrations, engine metal temperatures, lubricant temperature, engine control settings and initial engine spool acceleration. For piston engines, specify crankshaft speed, manifold pressure, cylinder thermodynamic states and ignition conditions.
7.bc: Prescribe engine inlet total pressure and total temperature, inlet flow distortion where relevant, fuel supply pressure and temperature, fuel composition, combustion wall thermal conditions, turbine cooling flows, exhaust backpressure, nozzle exit conditions, shaft torque demands, engine accessory loads, heat-transfer conditions and mechanical coupling to propellers, rotors or generators. Include combustor wall conditions, species inlet conditions and suitable outlet conditions for detailed reacting-flow simulations.
7.calibration: Calibrate compressor and turbine performance maps, combustion efficiency, pressure losses, fuel flow characteristics, heat-transfer coefficients, mechanical efficiencies, shaft losses, engine control parameters and transient response characteristics using component rig tests and complete engine test-cell measurements. Include temperature, pressure, rotational speed, fuel properties and operating altitude effects.
7.verification: Verify thermodynamic property calculations, conservation of mass and energy, compressor–turbine work matching, shaft power balance, engine cycle calculations, component map interpolation, combustion calculations and transient numerical integration. equations.models: Integrated computational architecture for all 26 suites

The 26 suites should operate as an integrated multidisciplinary aircraft simulation environment rather than as isolated numerical programs. Their shared computational foundation should include aircraft geometry and mesh representations, material and composite property databases, atmospheric and environmental models, propulsion characteristics, mass and inertia properties, aerodynamic coefficient databases, structural load transfer interfaces, coupled multiphysics solvers, time integration algorithms, optimisation algorithms, uncertainty quantification and common data exchange interfaces.

The numerical infrastructure should support finite volume methods, finite element methods, finite difference methods, spectral methods, boundary element methods, vortex methods, multibody dynamics, differential–algebraic equation solvers, ordinary differential equation solvers, nonlinear algebraic solvers, optimisation solvers, probabilistic methods and suitable reduced-order models.

For credible engineering implementation, the essential distinction is between governing physics, numerical discretisation, empirical closure models and validation evidence. Classical governing equations provide the physical foundations; constitutive laws and closure models represent material or unresolved physical behaviour; numerical methods approximate the solutions; and hybrid formulations couple disciplines or combine physics-based models with appropriately validated data-driven methods.

Aircraft certification and airworthiness substantiation should be treated as an additional cross-cutting function, not assumed to follow automatically from successful simulation. The attached document explicitly identifies verified models, validated predictions and traceable evidence as necessary elements of that capability.

The resulting architecture can support preliminary aircraft design, detailed engineering analysis, helicopter aeromechanics, multidisciplinary optimisation, operational mission simulation and aircraft techno-economic evaluation. However, each computational capability must be independently verified and validated within its intended operating envelope before its predictions can be regarded as sufficiently reliable for safety-critical engineering decisions.
ibcs: For the 26 suites to function as one comprehensive aircraft simulation platform, their initial states, operating conditions and boundary conditions must remain physically and numerically consistent.

The aerodynamic solver should supply pressure distributions, aerodynamic forces and moments to the structural, flight dynamics, aeroelastic and performance solvers. The structural solver should return deformation and stiffness information to the aerodynamic and aeroelastic solvers. The propulsion solver should provide thrust, torque, fuel consumption, heat generation and engine operating limits to the flight performance, thermal, mission and economic models. Rotorcraft solvers should exchange rotor inflow, blade motion, rotor loads, shaft torque and vibration states with the corresponding structural, drivetrain and flight dynamics solvers.

The flight control solver should exchange sensor estimates, commands and actuator responses with the aircraft dynamics solver. The icing solver should update aerodynamic geometry, surface conditions, mass distribution and thermal loads where relevant. The fuel and electrical systems should update aircraft mass, energy availability, heat generation and operating constraints. The mission simulation should integrate these outputs across the complete flight profile, while the economics suite should convert verified performance, utilisation, maintenance and energy-consumption predictions into life-cycle financial estimates.

A critical distinction for implementation: Not all 26 suites are governed by spatial partial differential equations. CFD, structural mechanics, heat transfer, acoustics and certain icing models require classical initial and boundary conditions. Flight dynamics, control systems, engine cycle models and electrical networks frequently use differential-algebraic initial-value formulations. Modal analyses use eigenvalue problems, while reliability, optimisation and economics use probabilistic, algebraic, constrained or time-dependent models. The computational architecture must therefore support the appropriate mathematical formulation for each suite rather than imposing one universal type of boundary condition.

Finally, the initial and boundary conditions listed here are typical engineering specifications, not an exhaustive case-by-case prescription or evidence of model validation. Specific aircraft configurations, operating regimes, numerical formulations and certification objectives determine which conditions are actually required and how they must be implemented.
cvv: Platform-wide calibration, verification and validation requirements

To make the 26 suites function as one integrated aircraft simulation platform, their calibration, verification and validation procedures should be connected through a common technical assurance framework.

Integrated calibration: Establish traceable material databases, aerodynamic coefficient databases, engine performance maps, rotor blade properties, structural characteristics, flight-test datasets, component reliability information and aircraft economic records. Each calibrated parameter should have documented units, provenance, uncertainty, operating range, estimation method and applicability limitations. Calibration datasets must be distinguished from datasets reserved for independent validation.

Integrated verification: Verify each numerical solver independently before assessing the coupled multiphysics platform. Subsequently verify data exchange, coordinate transformations, unit consistency, time synchronisation, aerodynamic load transfer, structural displacement transfer, propulsion coupling, control interfaces, thermal coupling, rotor dynamics integration and economic model integration. Include automated regression tests, conservation checks, numerical convergence assessments, software configuration management, reproducibility testing and continuous integration testing.

Integrated validation: Apply a hierarchical validation programme beginning with canonical mathematical and physical benchmarks, progressing through material and component experiments, subsystem tests, ground tests, wind-tunnel measurements, rotorcraft tests, complete aircraft flight tests and operational records. Validate both individual disciplinary predictions and coupled system responses. For example, aerodynamic loads should be evaluated independently before validating aeroelastic deformation; engine performance should be evaluated independently before validating complete mission fuel consumption; and mission performance should be evaluated before validating associated operating costs.

Uncertainty and credibility: Quantify input uncertainty, measurement uncertainty, parameter uncertainty, discretisation uncertainty, iterative uncertainty and model-form uncertainty wherever applicable. Establish separate acceptance criteria for exploratory research, preliminary design, detailed engineering, safety-critical analysis and certification substantiation. A model that is credible for conceptual aircraft design should not automatically be considered credible for flutter clearance, structural life prediction or flight safety decisions.

Certification and traceability: Maintain traceable links between engineering requirements, model assumptions, software versions, input datasets, calibration evidence, verification tests, validation experiments, uncertainty estimates and final engineering predictions. Where certification use is intended, align the evidence with the applicable airworthiness requirements and the relevant software, hardware, systems engineering and simulation assurance guidance.

Final engineering requirement: All 26 suites should undergo documented calibration where uncertain parameters require estimation, rigorous numerical and software verification, and independent validation appropriate to their intended applications. A successful numerical test suite establishes computational correctness within the tested scope, but it does not by itself establish physical predictive validity. Similarly, agreement with one experimental dataset does not demonstrate general validity across all aircraft configurations, flight regimes or operating conditions.

The resulting architecture provides a foundation for a verified, validated and uncertainty-quantified multidisciplinary aircraft engineering simulation platform, with demonstrated credibility determined separately for each model, coupled analysis and intended engineering application.

geometry: Mandatory universal geometry and mesh interoperability requirements
For the 26-suite platform to operate as an integrated aircraft engineering application, the following capabilities should be implemented across the entire system.

Geometry recognition and classification: The software shall identify whether an imported dataset represents exact CAD solids, open surfaces, shell geometry, tessellated surfaces, point clouds, implicit geometry, volumetric meshes, structural elements, aerodynamic grids or reduced-order representations. It shall classify aircraft components where metadata or reliable geometric recognition permits and allow manual correction when classification is uncertain.

Geometry healing and reconstruction: The software shall provide geometry inspection, tolerance checking, gap identification, duplicate removal, surface stitching, face orientation correction, non-manifold detection, intersection detection, topology repair and watertight reconstruction where appropriate. Any automated repair shall be traceable and shall not silently alter engineering-critical dimensions or features.

Mesh recognition and quality assurance: The software shall recognise supported mesh element types, connectivity, element order, boundary tags, cell zones, material regions and mesh partitions. It shall evaluate skewness, orthogonality, aspect ratio, Jacobian quality, element inversion, negative volumes, non-manifold connectivity and other solver-relevant quality measures before computation.

Automatic and user-controlled meshing: The application shall support surface meshing, volume meshing, boundary-layer meshing, structured and unstructured meshing, local refinement, curvature-based refinement, adaptive remeshing, mesh deformation, rotating interfaces and overset-grid preparation. Automatic meshing shall not imply that every valid CAD model can be meshed successfully without engineering intervention.

Geometry and mesh compatibility: Imported geometry and meshes shall be checked against the requirements of the selected computational suite. For example, aerodynamic CFD may require an appropriate fluid domain and boundary conditions, structural FEA may require valid element connectivity and material assignments, and aeroelasticity may require compatible fluid–structure coupling interfaces.

Units and coordinate systems: The software shall preserve or explicitly assign units, coordinate systems, aircraft reference axes, component coordinate frames, geometric scales, rotor axes, structural orientations and assembly transformations. Where units are absent or ambiguous, the importer shall request confirmation rather than silently assume a scale.

Assembly and metadata preservation: The software shall preserve component names, part identifiers, assembly hierarchies, material assignments, surface groups, mesh groups, boundary tags and other engineering metadata whenever supported by the source format. Where a format cannot represent required information, the application shall use companion metadata files or explicit user assignments.

High-fidelity and reduced-order modelling: The platform shall accommodate full three-dimensional geometry and meshes, two-dimensional sections, one-dimensional beam and network models, lumped-parameter representations, aerodynamic coefficient models and other reduced-order representations, provided the chosen analysis formulation supports them.

Geometry and mesh provenance: The application shall record source file information, import settings, geometry transformations, repairs, mesh generation settings, mesh quality results and model revisions to support repeatability, verification, validation and engineering auditability.

Universal import architecture: The platform shall use a modular importer and converter architecture rather than assuming that one geometry kernel or mesh reader can correctly interpret every format. Each supported format shall have a documented capability profile covering geometry entities, mesh element types, metadata preservation, limitations and validation tests.

The intended platform can be designed to accept a very broad range of conventional and unconventional aircraft geometries and meshes, regardless of the credible external CAD or meshing environment from which they originate. However, universal acceptance cannot be guaranteed merely by supporting a long list of file extensions.

A technically defensible requirement is that the application shall accept any physically realistic aircraft geometry or mesh that can be represented through a supported native format or a validated conversion pathway, provided that its topology, dimensions, mesh quality, physical metadata and numerical compatibility satisfy the requirements of the selected analysis.

This architecture would allow the 26 engineering suites to share a common geometry and mesh foundation while retaining the specialised physical models, discretisations, boundary conditions and verification requirements needed for credible aircraft engineering simulations.
geometry_intro: The following expands the document into a geometry and mesh interoperability specification. The document identifies the engineering analyses but does not itself prescribe CAD formats, mesh formats or import standards.
